name: Sum of Medians
description: In one well-known algorithm of finding the k -th order statistics we should divide all elements into groups of five consecutive elements and find the median of each five. A median is called the middle element of a sorted array (it's the third largest element for a group of five). To increase the algorithm's performance speed on a modern video card, you should be able to find a sum of medians in each five of the array. A sum of medians of a sorted k -element set S = { a 1 , a 2 , ..., a k } , where a 1 < a 2 < a 3 < ... < a k , will be understood by as The operator stands for taking the remainder, that is stands for the remainder of dividing x by y . To organize exercise testing quickly calculating the sum of medians for a changing set was needed.
input_specification: The first line contains number n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ), the number of operations performed. Then each of n lines contains the description of one of the three operations: add x — add the element x to the set; del x — delete the element x from the set; sum — find the sum of medians of the set. For any add x operation it is true that the element x is not included in the set directly before the operation. For any del x operation it is true that the element x is included in the set directly before the operation. All the numbers in the input are positive integers, not exceeding 10 9 .
output_specification: For each operation sum print on the single line the sum of medians of the current set. If the set is empty, print 0. Please, do not use the %lld specificator to read or write 64-bit integers in C++. It is preferred to use the cin , cout streams (also you may use the %I64d specificator).

approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 85D — Sum of Medians [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
